2116: Fat was low in all treatments, as anticipated for a steamed product, ranging from 0.28% in KI and GCI to 0.17% in GBI and RBI (Table 4.108). The carrot-fortified treatments were marginally higher, the carotenoids of carrot being extracted along with the lipid during Soxhlet extraction (Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001). Ash ranged from 5.21% in GBI to 2.47% in DI (Table 4.109) and was highest in the beet-fortified treatment of every variety, beetroot contributing an appreciable quantity of minerals (Chhikara et al., 2019).
2117: Phytate is the principal anti-nutritional factor of cereal and pulse foods, since it chelates divalent cations and renders them unavailable (Reddy et al., 1982; Haug and Lantzsch, 1983). It ranged from 2.52 mg g⁻¹ in KBI to 0.82 mg g⁻¹ in GI (Table 4.110) and was highest in the beet-fortified treatments. All values were substantially lower than those customarily reported for raw rice and black gram, phytase derived from the grain and from the microflora degrading phytate during soaking and fermentation (Lestienne et al., 2005; Gupta et al., 2015). The mineral gain conferred by fortification is therefore partly offset by a concomitant rise in phytate. What governs absorption is the phytate-to-mineral ratio rather than the mineral content alone (Hemalatha et al., 2007).
2202: The lower predicted glycaemic index of the carrot-fortified idli accords with recent work on fibre-rich substitution in the same food. Sajayan et al. (2024) replaced part of the rice in idli batter with dried jackfruit bulb and recorded a lower starch hydrolysis index together with higher radical-scavenging activity and a larger lactic acid bacterial population, without loss of acceptability at moderate levels of substitution. Beetroot behaves comparably in other cereal foods: Mitrevski et al. (2025) determined that biscuits containing 20% beetroot powder returned a glycaemic index of 49 and carried more potassium, phosphorus, zinc and betaine than the control while remaining the most preferred sample in sensory evaluation.
2204: The interaction was highly significant for all the bioactive fractions, Kalojira with beet extract constituting the superior combination for each. Total phenol, determined by the Folin-Ciocalteu method (Kaur and Kapoor, 2002), ranged from 290.97 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in KBI to 53.47 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in DI (Table 4.111), a differential exceeding fivefold. Total flavonoid, determined by the aluminium chloride method (Chang et al., 2002), ranged from 171.34 to 42.95 mg QE 100 g⁻¹ (Table 4.112), and total antioxidant activity from 426.88 to 165.26 mg TE 100 g⁻¹ (Table 4.113).
2205: Two factors generated this variation. The first is variety. Pigmented rice grains contain substantially more phenolic acid and flavonoid than white grains, the pericarp of black rice being particularly rich in them (Zhang et al., 2010; Sompong et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2014). Goufo and Trindade (2014) likewise reported that the antioxidant capacity of rice derives principally from the bound phenolics of the bran layer, which is why the black-husked Kalojira retained its lead in every product form. The greater secondary metabolite content of aromatic landraces relative to non-aromatic types (Ghosh and Roychoudhury, 2018) was likewise evident in the present data.
2206: The second factor is the fortifying material. Beetroot is among the richest sources of betalain pigments and additionally carries phenolic acids (Ravichandran et al., 2013; Chhikara et al., 2019). Betalains are reasonably stable at the mildly acidic pH generated by lactic fermentation, so that most of the added pigment survived steaming. The beet-fortified treatments were consequently consistently high in phenol and antioxidant activity. The magnitude of the gain differed between varieties, which accounts for the significant interaction.
2207: Beta-carotene derived almost entirely from carrot, ranging from 45.77 in KCI and 43.59 in GCI to nil in every plain treatment (Table 4.114). Carrot ranks among the richest sources of provitamin A carotenoids, and its all-trans β-carotene is well retained under moist heat such as steaming, unlike frying or protracted dry heating (Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Sharma et al., 2012). Anthocyanin exhibited the converse pattern, being detected only in the beet-fortified treatments, from 1.86 in KBI to 0.98 in DBI (Table 4.115). It derives from the betacyanin of beetroot together with pigment carried over from the black husk of Kalojira (Sompong et al., 2011). KCI may therefore be employed for a provitamin A-rich product and KBI for an anthocyanin-rich product (Bagchi et al., 2020).
2244: The interaction was significant for all five minerals. Copper ranged from 0.97 ppm in GBI to 0.21 ppm in KCI and DI (Table 4.116) and iron from 3.36 ppm in RI to 1.36 ppm in DI (Table 4.117). Zinc ranged from 0.89 ppm in RI to 0.64 ppm in DI (Table 4.118) and manganese from 0.69 ppm in GI to 0.37 ppm in DI (Table 4.119). Manganese merits particular note, since the interaction was significant notwithstanding the non-significance of the main effect of fortification, which demonstrates that the response to the extract was contingent upon variety.
2245: Calcium varied most widely, from 550.88 ppm in GBI to 61.44 ppm in KI (Table 4.120). The beet-fortified treatment was highest in every variety, followed by the carrot-fortified treatment. Beetroot constitutes a useful source of calcium and other minerals for cereal foods (Chhikara et al., 2019). This gain is of consequence, since rice-based diets are poor in calcium (Rani et al., 2006).
2246: The mineral results must be interpreted in conjunction with the phytate values. Phytate chelates calcium, iron and zinc in the gut, forming complexes that are poorly absorbed, and a phytate-to-zinc molar ratio exceeding fifteen indicates poor zinc availability (Reddy et al., 1982; Hemalatha et al., 2007). Soaking and fermentation activate phytase and remove a substantial proportion of the phytate, thereby improving the availability of iron and zinc in the finished product (Lestienne et al., 2005; Gupta et al., 2015). Among the twelve combinations, the plain and carrot-fortified treatments of Gobindabhog combined good mineral content with low phytate and are therefore superior from the standpoint of mineral availability.
2282: The rise in calcium and other minerals under beet fortification corresponds to the mineral enrichment that Mitrevski et al. (2025) reported for beetroot powder in a cereal product, in which potassium, phosphorus and zinc all increased with the level of addition.
2284: Colour is the attribute a consumer perceives first and exerts a strong influence on the acceptance of a fermented cereal product (Amerine et al., 1965; Pathare et al., 2013). Lightness ranged from 72.92 in DI to 36.47 in DBI (Table 4.121), declining within every variety in the order plain, carrot-fortified, beet-fortified. Redness rose from -1.81 in DI to 13.26 in DCI (Table 4.122) and yellowness declined from 110.98 in DI to 59.45 in DBI (Table 4.123).
2285: The total colour difference ranged from 45.02 in RCI to 28.70 in RI (Table 4.124). These values lie far above the threshold of approximately three units at which a colour change becomes perceptible to an untrained eye (Pathare et al., 2013). The hue angle shifted from -90.21 in GI towards the red region in the fortified treatments (Table 4.125), and chroma declined from 110.83 in DI to 59.72 in DBI (Table 4.126), indicating that the fortified products were darker but not less saturated.
2286: These changes follow from the pigment chemistry of the two vegetables. The betacyanin of beetroot imparts an intense red to violet colour that is reasonably stable at the mildly acidic pH of the fermented batter and survives brief steaming, though it degrades under protracted or dry heating (Ravichandran et al., 2013; Chhikara et al., 2019). The carotenoids of carrot impart an orange to yellow colour, are more thermostable, and elevate redness without depressing lightness to the same degree (Rodriguez-Amaya, 2001; Sharma et al., 2012). Kalojira yielded a darker product in every form on account of pigment carried over from the black husk (Sompong et al., 2011). The high appearance scores of the fortified products, discussed below, indicate that the panel favoured this colour change.
2330: The texture of idli is contingent upon the gas-holding capacity of the fermented batter, which in turn depends upon the interaction between the globulin and arabinogalactan of black gram and the gelatinised starch of rice (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005). Hardness ranged from 147.73 in KI to 45.09 in DI (Table 4.127). The plain product was the hardest in every variety, demonstrating that the addition of a vegetable extract dilutes the starch and protein network and yields a more tender product.
2331: Adhesiveness was least negative in DI (-0.19) and most negative in RI (-19.58) (Table 4.128). Springiness ranged from 1.04 in DI to 0.46 in KBI (Table 4.129), cohesiveness from 0.94 in KI to 0.40 in KBI (Table 4.130) and resilience from 0.55 in GI to 0.19 in RBI (Table 4.133). Gumminess and chewiness are computed from hardness and cohesiveness (Bourne, 2002) and therefore followed the same pattern, the highest values of 11890.93 and 10263.60 occurring in KI (Tables 4.131 and 4.132) and the lowest in KBI.
2332: The association between amylose and hardness merits note. The plain treatments carried the most amylose and were likewise the hardest and most cohesive, amylose retrograding and forming a firm gel network as the product cools (Tester et al., 2004; Mohapatra and Bal, 2006). The fortified treatments, in which amylose was diluted, yielded a softer and less chewy product. These instrumental values correspond to the texture scores awarded by the panel, which supports the contention of Szczesniak (2002) that instrumental texture analysis of a steamed cereal product accords closely with panel judgement.
2383: The sensory data were recorded by a semi-trained panel on a nine-point hedonic scale following Amerine et al. (1965) and Meilgaard et al. (2007). Aroma was highest in GI (7.70), which was at par with GCI (7.25), and lowest in KCI (5.65) and DI (5.72) (Table 4.134). This demonstrates that the aroma of the landraces, deriving principally from 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (Buttery et al., 1983; Bhattacharjee et al., 2002), survives soaking, grinding, fermentation and steaming. The lower aroma scores of the fortified treatments within each aromatic variety indicate that the vegetable extract partly masks the natural aroma of the rice, notwithstanding its improvement of colour and taste (Ghosh and Roychoudhury, 2018).
2384: Flavour exhibited a significant interaction and ranged from 7.96 in KBI to 5.46 in DI (Table 4.136). The interaction was non-significant for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability (Tables 4.135, 4.137 to 4.140). This constitutes an important finding, since it indicates that the sensory gain conferred by fortification was uniform across all four varieties and is not confined to any one landrace. Overall acceptability was highest in KBI (8.64), followed by KCI (8.24), and lowest in DI (6.14).
2385: The higher scores of the fortified treatments for appearance and overall acceptability follow from the colour results, a natural pigment markedly improving the appearance of a white steamed product (Pathare et al., 2013). The higher texture scores follow from the instrumental data, the panel having preferred the softer and less chewy products. Comparable gains in consumer preference following the addition of pigment-rich cereal and vegetable fractions to traditional Indian foods have been reported by Pal et al. (2019) and Bagchi et al. (2020). The present results demonstrate that the aromatic landraces of West Bengal may be converted into an attractive and nutritionally superior fermented food without recourse to any synthetic colour or additive.
2436: The relations among the forty two quality parameters were examined by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient over twenty four treatment means, namely the twelve treatment combinations in each of the two years. The full correlation matrix is presented as a heat map in Fig. 4.98, and the correlation of overall acceptability with every other parameter is given in Table 4.141. At twenty two degrees of freedom the critical values of r are 0.404 at the 5% level and 0.515 at the 1% level (Snedecor and Cochran, 1994).
2437: The three bioactive fractions were closely associated. Total phenol correlated with total flavonoid (r = 0.983) and with total antioxidant activity (r = 0.971), and total flavonoid with total antioxidant activity (r = 0.945), all three coefficients being significant at the 1% level. This indicates that the antioxidant potential of the product derives almost entirely from its phenolic and flavonoid content, which accords with Zhang et al. (2010), Sompong et al. (2011) and Goufo and Trindade (2014). Total soluble protein likewise correlated with total phenol (r = 0.767) and phytate with total phenol (r = 0.632); protein, phytate and bound phenolic acids all co-occur in the aleurone and sub-aleurone layers of the grain (Reddy et al., 1982).
2438: The carbohydrate fractions were negatively correlated with the bioactive fractions. Total carbohydrate was negatively correlated with total phenol (r = -0.913) and starch with total antioxidant activity (r = -0.955), both significant at the 1% level. Total carbohydrate was itself correlated with starch (r = 0.895) and amylose (r = 0.824), and lightness with yellowness (r = 0.995) and with total carbohydrate (r = 0.832). All these relations express a single underlying gradient, namely the replacement of the starchy rice base by the pigment-rich vegetable extract. The fortified products were consequently at once darker, lower in starch and richer in antioxidants.
